level1.text: $1.8\,\text{kg}$ of water at a temperature of $12\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ is poured into the tank of a coffee maker. The coffee maker heats the water to $96\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How large is the quantity of heat transferred to the water? Give the answer in megajoules.

A cast-iron frying pan of mass $2.4\,\text{kg}$ is lifted from the stove onto a table in a cabin. The temperature of the pan falls from $220\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $25\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How large a quantity of heat does the pan give out to the surroundings? Give the answer in kilojoules.

A children's sandpit contains $50\,\text{kg}$ of sand. During the morning the Sun heats the sand from $14\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $32\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How large is the quantity of heat transferred to the sand? Give the answer in kilojoules.

A cabin hot tub contains $1200\,\text{kg}$ of water. During the night the water cools from $38.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $31.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How large is the quantity of heat $Q$ transferred to the water? Give the answer with its sign in megajoules (a negative $Q$ means that the water gives out heat).

A $0.50\,\text{kg}$ bag of ice from the freezer is put into a cool bag. The temperature of the ice rises from $-22\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $-4.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and the ice does not melt yet. How large is the quantity of heat transferred to the ice? Give the answer in kilojoules.
At the beach, sunlight gives $1.0\,\text{kg}$ of water and $1.0\,\text{kg}$ of dry sand the same quantity of heat. The sand warms clearly more than the water. What explains this?
level1.answer: The specific heat capacity of water is greater, so the same quantity of heat raises its temperature less.

choices.text: Water reflects the sunlight back, so less heat is transferred to it than to the sand.
choices.feedback: In the task the water and the sand receive the same quantity of heat, so reflection does not explain the difference. The water also warms, just less.

choices.text: The change in temperature depends only on the mass and the quantity of heat, so the substance does not affect it.
choices.feedback: The substance does matter: the formula $Q = c m \Delta T$ contains the specific heat capacity $c$, which is different for different substances. So the same $Q$ and the same $m$ give different substances a different $\Delta T$.

choices.text: Sand is denser than water, so the same quantity of heat raises its temperature more.
choices.feedback: Density does not decide, because the masses are the same. The formula $\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{c m}$ contains the mass $m$, not the density, and the difference comes from the specific heat capacity $c$ of the substance. The $c = 4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$ of water is greater than the $800\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$ of sand.

choices.text: The specific heat capacity of water is greater, so the same quantity of heat raises its temperature less.
choices.feedback: Correct: the change in temperature is $\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{c m}$. When $Q$ and $m$ are the same, a large $c$ means a small $\Delta T$. The $c = 4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$ of water is about five times the value of sand, $800\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$.

level1.text: A copper coffee pot has a mass of $0.50\,\text{kg}$. The pot receives a quantity of heat of $15\,\text{kJ}$ from the stove, and no heat is transferred from the pot to the surroundings. By how many kelvins does the temperature of the pot rise?

An aluminium saucepan has a mass of $0.60\,\text{kg}$.

a) Calculate the heat capacity $C$ of the saucepan.

b) How large a quantity of heat is needed to heat the saucepan from $18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ to $78\,{}^\circ\text{C}$? Give the result of part b) in kilojoules in the answer box.

level2.text: $160\,\text{g}$ of water at a temperature of $95\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ is poured into a mug. The tea is too hot to drink, so $40\,\text{g}$ of cold water at a temperature of $8.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ is added. What is the temperature of the water after mixing? Assume that no heat is transferred to the mug or the air.

An electric heater heats a metal object of mass $0.50\,\text{kg}$ at a constant power of $100\,\text{W}$. The graph shows the temperature of the object as a function of time. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal? Read the values you need from the graph and assume that all the energy of the heater is transferred to the object.

A hot-water tank in a cabin contains $80\,\text{kg}$ of water at a temperature of $9.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The electric resistor of the tank gives out a quantity of heat of $15\,\text{MJ}$ to the water. What is the final temperature of the water, when heat losses are not taken into account?

An aluminium ladle of mass $0.25\,\text{kg}$ and temperature $95\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ has warmed up on the sauna benches. The ladle is dropped into a bucket that contains $0.40\,\text{kg}$ of water at a temperature of $18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. What is the common final temperature of the water and the ladle? Assume that no heat is transferred to the bucket or the air.

In a calorimeter, $0.50\,\text{kg}$ of an unknown liquid is heated with an electric resistor at a constant power of $100\,\text{W}$. The temperature is measured at one-minute intervals, and the results are in the table (example data). Assume that all the energy of the resistor is transferred to the liquid.

a) In the temperature–time graph, draw a straight line that fits the points. The line passes approximately through the points $(0\,\text{s};\ 20.0\,{}^\circ\text{C})$ and $(300\,\text{s};\ 34.5\,{}^\circ\text{C})$. Use the slope of the line to calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid.

b) Which liquid is it? Justify your answer with the $c$ values of the table.

c) Name one way to reduce heat losses in an experiment like this and justify why it improves the result.

Give the result of part a) in the answer box.

data.caption: Temperature of the liquid during heating (example data)

level2.text:
Two liquids, A and B, are heated in two identical calorimeters with an electric resistor of the same power. Each contains $0.40\,\text{kg}$ of liquid. One liquid is water and the other is oil. The temperatures are measured at half-minute intervals (example data). Assume that all the energy of the resistor is transferred to the liquid.

a) Which liquid is water? Justify your answer.

b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of the oil using the table value for water. Compare the rises in temperature of the liquids in $120\,\text{s}$.

Give the result of part b) in the answer box.

data.caption: Temperatures of the liquids during heating (example data)

level2.text:
A $0.20\,\text{kg}$ copper object at a temperature of $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ is dropped into an insulated vessel that contains $0.50\,\text{kg}$ of water at a temperature of $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The heat capacity of the vessel itself and the heat losses are ignored.

The student's solution: “The temperatures even out, so the final temperature is the mean of the initial temperatures: $(100 + 20) : 2 = 60\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.”

a) Explain why the student's solution is wrong.

b) Calculate the correct final temperature.

Give the result of part b) in the answer box.

level3.text: In the old days the washing water in a smoke sauna was heated by dropping hot stones from the stove into a wooden bucket. The bucket holds $20\,\text{kg}$ of lake water at a temperature of $10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and the stove has heated the stones to $300\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How many kilograms of stones must be dropped into the bucket so that the temperature of the water rises to $40\,{}^\circ\text{C}$? The specific heat capacity of the stones is $800\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$. Assume that no heat is transferred to the bucket or the air and that no water vaporises. Justify what the final temperature of the stones is.

At a cabin shore there is a shallow bay with an area of $2000\,\text{m}^2$ and a mean depth of $1.2\,\text{m}$. On a sunny summer day the water of the bay receives energy of $18\,\text{MJ}$ from the Sun for each square metre of the surface. A cubic metre of water has a mass of $1000\,\text{kg}$. Assume that the energy stays in the water and the water mixes evenly. By how many kelvins does the temperature of the water in the bay rise during the day? Also justify why the result does not depend on the area of the bay.

A heat store is being planned for a cabin, in which summer solar heat is stored. The options are $1.0\,\text{m}^3$ of water, whose mass is $1000\,\text{kg}$, or dry sand, of which there is $1600\,\text{kg}$ in a cubic metre. The temperature of each store varies between $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and $70\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How many cubic metres of sand are needed for it to store as much energy as the water store? Justify why the ratio of the volumes is smaller than the ratio of the specific heat capacities.

In a calorimeter, $0.50\,\text{kg}$ of water is heated with an electric resistor at a constant power of $200\,\text{W}$. The temperature of the water is measured at one-minute intervals (example data). The room temperature is $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The heat capacity of the vessel itself is ignored.

a) Calculate the specific heat capacity of water from the measurement of the first minute, assuming that the heat losses are still negligible, and compare it with the table value.

b) Explain why the graph curves although the power is constant, and justify why the specific heat capacity should be fitted to the beginning of the graph.

c) Use the table value for water and calculate the mean power of the heat loss in the interval $480\text{–}600\,\text{s}$. Give the result of part c) in watts in the answer box.

data.caption: Temperature of the water during heating (example data)

level3.text:
An uninsulated mug contains $0.300\,\text{kg}$ of hot water. The room temperature is $20.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The temperature of the water is measured at ten-minute intervals (example data). The heat capacity of the mug and evaporation are ignored. According to the proposed model, the thermal power given out by the water is directly proportional to the difference in temperature between the water and the room: $P = k\,(T_\text{mean} - T_\text{room})$, where $T_\text{mean}$ is the mean temperature of the water in the interval under consideration.

a) Calculate the quantity of heat given out by the water and the mean thermal power in each ten-minute interval.

b) Calculate the coefficient $k$ for each interval. Give $k$ of the first interval in the answer box.

c) On the basis of the $k$ values, evaluate whether the model fits the measurements, and justify why the cooling of the water slows down.
